nodes.name: Heteroatom-induced oriented growth of Ni-WO3
nodes.procedure: Ni-doped WO3 precursor (denoted as Ni-WO3) supported on carbon cloth (CC) was prepared via a heteroatom-induced oriented-growth strategy, in which ammonium metatungstate (AMT) was selected as a W source and Ni2+ ions were chosen as a structural additive. The Ni-WO3 features mirror-symmetric nanoarrays with 5% Ni input showing highly sturdy network structure assembled by intergrown mirror-symmetric nanoarrays.
nodes.source_text: As schematically illustrated in Figure 1a, the mirror-symmetric nanoarray networks... ammonium metatungstate (AMT) was selected as a W source and Ni2+ ions were chosen as a structural additive... Herein, we chose the mirror-symmetric nanoarrays of Ni-WO3 with 5% Ni input as a typical example.

nodes.name: Nitriding by chemical vapor deposition
nodes.procedure: Ni-WO3 was nitrided by chemical vapor deposition with melamine as an N source to obtain Ni-WNO. Figure 1k displays the inconspicuous morphological change from Ni-WO3 to Ni-WNO and the uniform distribution of N in Ni-WNO, indicating the successful nitridation of Ni-WO3 and the good thermal robustness of the resultant Ni-WNO with the mirror-symmetric nanoarray structure.
nodes.source_text: Subsequently, Ni-WO3 was nitrided by chemical vapor deposition with melamine as an N source to obtain Ni-WNO (Figure S6).

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni-WO3 shows distinct diffraction signals of hexagonal WO3 (h-WO3, JCPDS No. 85-2460), with Ni dopants increasing the diffraction intensity of the (200) facet relative to the (002) facet.
nodes.evidence_snippet: X-ray diffraction (XRD) was first conducted to gain the structural information of Ni - WO3 . The obtained materials show distinct diffraction signals of hexagonal WO3 ( h - WO3 , JCPDS No. 85-2460), and the introduction of Ni dopants mainly increases the diffraction intensity of the (200) facet relative to the (002) facet (Figure S1).

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni-WO3 features mirror-symmetric nanoarray networks assembled by intergrown hexagonal sheets and nanorods, with 5% Ni input showing highly sturdy network structure.
nodes.evidence_snippet: the SEM images in Figure 1f clearly confirm its highly sturdy network structure assembled by the intergrown mirror-symmetric nanoarrays as indicated by the white circle regions in Figure 1f2

nodes.characterization_summary: HAADF-STEM images of Ni-WO3 nanorod along <010> direction show growth in c-axis (001) orientation with less intense atomic columns at bridging sites identified as atomically dispersed Ni atoms.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Figure 1h shows the high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) images of a representative Ni- WO3 nanorod acquired along the < 010> direction, which indicates that the growth of the lateral Ni - WO 3 nanorods is in a c -axis (001) orientation.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni-WNO shows clear diffraction peaks of cubic WNO (JCPDS No. 25-1254) with compressive strain due to Ni dopants.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In Figure 2a, Ni-WNO shows clear diffraction peaks of the cubic WNO (JCPDS No. 25-1254) with compressive strain due to the dopants of Ni.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni-WNO shows Raman signals at 680 and 800 cm⁻¹ for symmetric stretching vibration (νs) of O-W-O, with additional binding mode at 883 cm⁻¹ attributed to lattice mismatch of W-O-Ni stretching induced by Ni dopants.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In Figure 2b, Raman signals at 680 and 800 cm⁻¹ in both WNO and Ni-WNO are associated with the symmetric stretching vibration (νs) of O-W-O. Conspicuously, Ni-WNO displays an additional binding mode centered at 883 cm⁻¹ , which could be attributed to the lattice mismatch of W-O-Ni stretching induced by Ni dopants.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni-WNO W 4f XPS shows W⁶⁺ (37.7/35.5 eV) and W⁴⁺ (34.2/32.2 eV) associated with tungsten oxynitride species; Ni 2p shows Niⁿ⁺ (n>0) at 870.4/853.3 eV vs Ni CS Ni⁰ at 869.9/852.5 eV.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In the deconvoluted W 4f XPS peaks (Table S2), the pair peaks in Ni-WNO at 37.7 and 35.5 eV are ascribed to the W 4f5/2 and W 4f7/2 of W6+ , respectively, while the pair peaks at lower binding energy (34.2 and 32.2 eV) can be assigned to the W 4f5/2 and W 4f7/2 of W4+ , which are associated with the formation of tungsten oxynitride species. In the fitted Ni 2p (Table S3), the pair peaks in Ni CS at 869.9 and 852.5 eV are ascribed to Ni 2p1/2 and Ni 2p3/2 of Ni0 , indicating the phase formation of metallic species.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni K-edge XANES: Ni foil ≈ Ni CS < Ni-WNO < Ni(OH)₂ indicating Ni-WNO average Ni valence between 0 and +2; W L₃-edge XANES shows Ni-WNO higher W oxidation state than WNO but lower than WO₃.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In XANES profiles (Figure 2c), the Ni K-edge position follows the order of Ni foil ≈ Ni CS < Ni-WNO < Ni(OH)2 , which indicates that the average valence state of nickel (Ni n+ ) in Ni-WNO lies between 0 and +2 . Conspicuously, Ni-WNO exhibits a much lower white line intensity relative to the WO3 counterpart, but marginally higher than WNO, demonstrating that the incorporation of Ni results in a higher oxidation state of W in Ni-WNO.

nodes.characterization_summary: FT-EXAFS: Ni-WNO Ni-N/O at 1.65 Å (not phase-corrected), no Ni-Ni path confirming atomic Ni dispersion; W-N/O at 1.62 Å (phase-corrected 1.92 Å) for WNO, shorter W-W/Ni paths in Ni-WNO indicating compressive strain.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In FT-EXAFS profiles (Figure 2d), a broad peak appears at 1.65 Å (not phase-corrected) with a prominent shoulder on the low- R side, which is associated with Ni-N and Ni-O single scattering. Meanwhile, the absence of Ni-Ni path verifies the atomically dispersed Ni sites in the Ni-WNO. In the case of WNO, an obvious peak in the R -space at 1.62 Å (phase-corrected: 1.92 Å) is associated with the W-N/O coordination, while peaks at about 2.47 and 2.90 Å (phase-corrected: 2.79 and 3.20 Å) could be assigned to the W-W scattering path. However, Ni-WNO exhibits a shorter W-W/Ni scattering path at about 2.30 and 2.86 Å (phase-corrected: 2.67 and 3.16 Å)

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni-WNO composed of Ni-incorporated WNO nanocrystals with average size of 4 nm.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images (Figure 2h,i), it can be observed that Ni-WNO is composed of Ni-incorporated WNO nanocrystals with an average size of about 4 nm (the inset of Figure 2i).

nodes.characterization_summary: SAED pattern of Ni-WNO matches cubic WNO phase without crystalline Ni particles or clusters.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern of Ni-WNO and the corresponding extracted intensity profile match well with the cubic WNO phase without any signal of crystalline Ni particles or clusters

nodes.characterization_summary: Atomic resolution HAADF-STEM confirms Ni atoms highly dispersed in Ni-WNO matrix.
nodes.evidence_snippet: This could be further verified by the atomic resolution HAADF-STEM images (Figure 2k,l) and energy dispersive spectroscopic (EDS) elemental mappings of Ni-WNO (Figures 2m and S13).

nodes.characterization_summary: EDS elemental mappings confirm uniform distribution of elements in Ni-WNO.
nodes.evidence_snippet: energy dispersive spectroscopic (EDS) elemental mappings of Ni-WNO (Figures 2m and S13)

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni-WNO shows inconspicuous morphological change from Ni-WO3 with uniform N distribution, indicating successful nitridation and good thermal robustness.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Figure 1k displays the inconspicuous morphological change from Ni - WO3 to WNO and the uniform distribution of N in Ni-WNO, indicating the successful nitridation of Ni - WO3 and the good thermal robustness of the resultant Ni-WNO

nodes.characterization_summary: WT-EXAFS confirms atomic dispersion of Ni in Ni-WNO (max at 1.6 Å, 6.1 Å⁻¹ for N/O coordination) and increased metallic feature vs WNO.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Further wavelet transform (WT)-EXAFS analysis was applied to visualize and distinguish scatterers according to their atomic weight (Figure 2g). Conspicuously, the intensity maximum (1.6 Å, 6.1 Å⁻¹ ) in Ni-WNO matches well with the scattering by directly coordinated light atoms (N, O)

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni-WNO O K-edge NEXAFS shows increased oxygen vacancy content vs WNO as evidenced by increased superoxide species (O₂⁻, 534.3 eV) intensity.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Correspondingly, near-edge X-ray absorption fine structure (NEXAFS) profiles at the O K-edge were also provided to present additional information on the structural alterations between Ni-WNO and WNO from the perspective of coordinated O atoms (Figure S12a). Hereinto, Ni-WNO shows considerably increased oxygen vacancy content as evidenced by the increased intensity of the characteristic band of superoxide species (O2-, 534.3 eV)

nodes.characterization_summary: EPR confirms increased oxygen vacancy content in Ni-WNO.
nodes.evidence_snippet: and electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) signals (Figure S12b)
